status.description: What the supervisor has observed of this instance, written by the server and ignored on a write.

switch_off.description: When the host switches a service module off because it keeps failing. A key left out follows the server's core.modules_switch_off. Only a service module takes it. The write replaces the whole spec, so a client that leaves it out returns the module to the server's setting.

type.description: The registered implementation this instance is built from, either a bare name or a namespace and a name separated by one /. Fixed at creation: changing it is remove and add.

ui.description: For an enabled and ready module whose manifest carries a ui block, what the frontend needs to load it. Absent otherwise.

uid.description: Host-minted identity. Data rows reference it, and nothing changes it after creation.

version.description: Fencing token, covering the whole overlay. Quote the ETag in If-Match on a write.

configurable.description: Whether instances are declared in configuration.

deprecated.description: Present only for an entry on its way out. It names the application release the deprecation shipped in and the entry to move to, when one takes over. The entry keeps being served until a later release removes it.

kind.description: The kind, as it is written in a ref, a path and a metric label.

runtimes.description: What an instance of this kind may declare under runtime.

summary.description: What instances of the kind are.

runtimes.description: The set an instance's runtime key is drawn from.

version.description: The content version of the set.

vocabulary.description: The vocabulary this set belongs to.

at.description: When the host read the line.

split.description: Whether the line continues in the next entry, because it was too long to keep whole.

text.description: The line as the module wrote it.

budget_bytes.description: The memory the module's process may use, in bytes.

budget_source.description: Who set the budget: the operator with memory_mib, the module's author in its manifest, or the server default.

failures_in_window.description: How many failed starts and stops count against the module inside the switch-off window of switch_off_window_seconds.

held_until_restart.description: Whether the module stays off until the server restarts.

last_stop.description: Why the process last stopped. Absent when it has not stopped.

near_budget.description: Whether the process is close to its budget.

on_over_memory.description: What the host does over the budget, as in force: stop or warn.

over_budget.description: Whether the last reading was over the budget. Only a module with on_over_memory warn keeps running in this state.

switch_off_failures.description: How many failed starts or stops inside the window switch the module off, as in force. 0 never switches it off.

switch_off_source.description: Who set the switch-off: the operator with switch_off on the spec, or the server default.

switch_off_window_seconds.description: How far back failed starts and stops count, in seconds, as in force.

switched_off.description: Present when the host switched the module off because it kept stopping.

used_bytes.description: The memory the process uses now, in bytes. Absent when the host cannot read it.

items.description: The readings, oldest first. One every two seconds while the module has run.

stops.description: The failed stops the host still counts, oldest first, inside the window of the readings.

allowed_origins.description: The browser origins this module adds to the ones the API answers. A page served from one may call the API from a browser while this instance is switched on. Absent when none is granted.

asked.description: What the install granted: the permissions, events and records room the release asked for when an operator approved it. Absent for an install without approval, which leaves the module switched off; switching such a module on starts it with nothing granted.

author.description: Who answers for this module, from its manifest's codeowner key.

conflicts.description: The releases of other modules this module refuses to run beside, from its manifest's conflict, each with the constraint and the release this server has.

database.description: The database of its own this instance was granted. Absent when it was granted none.

listening.description: The ports this instance may listen on now, by the name its manifest gave each, with the reason from the manifest. A port the operator moved carries the number it was moved to. Absent when no port is granted.

options.description: The settings this module reads, each with its type, its default and what it does. The config block of this instance overrides a key only where it writes that key.

pulled.description: True when an install added this module because another module requires it, and false when the operator asked for it.

requires.description: What the module declared it cannot run without. The server checks each entry before it starts the instance. An entry on another module carries the release this server has of it.

suggests.description: The modules this module works better with, from its manifest's suggest, each with the reason. A suggestion installs nothing.

examples: Counts what each print used and warns before a spool runs out.

default.description: What this key is worth when the config block leaves it out. Empty for a required key, and for a secret, whose value is never published.

key.description: The key as an operator writes it under this instance's config block.

required.description: The module does not start until this key is written. A required key has no default.

summary.description: One line saying what this key does.
examples: How often the readings collected since the last report go up.

hidden.description: Whether the page is kept out of the sidebar. Its route still works.

icon.description: The icon the sidebar entry draws, and absent for the default.

path.description: The last segment of the route, one DNS label.

reason.description: For a suggestion, why the module is suggested, from the manifest.

since.description: The contract version that introduced the requirement, when the module said.

state.description: The state of that instance, such as ready or failed. Absent with installed.

runtime.description: The runtime, as it is written under the runtime key.

summary.description: What is behind an instance that declares it.

devices.description: On a device slot, the devices the entry is drawn for. Absent for every device.

title.description: What the section heading or the settings tab reads.

contributes.description: What the bundle may register. A registration outside it is refused.

role.description: The role this account is to hold: viewer, operator or admin.

pattern.description: The pattern the router matches on.

reason.description: Why this path is not a published operation.

bytes_sent.description: How many of the file's bytes this server has put on the wire. A byte the printer asks for again counts once.

bytes_total.description: The file's length as this server measured it before the first byte left.

can_stop.description: True when the caller holds operate on the printer, which is what the stop route takes.

device_id.description: The printer the file is going to.

ended_at.description: When it ended, as an RFC 3339 string. Absent while it runs.

mine.description: True when the caller's own request began the transfer, from any browser or client.

path.description: Where the file lands on the printer, storage-prefixed.

printer_name.description: The printer's name as the printer listing shows it.

started_at.description: When it began, as an RFC 3339 string.

started_by.description: The principal whose request began the transfer, such as user:ada. Present only for a caller holding view_audit on the printer, because who asked is audit.

state.description: One of queued, sending, done, failed, cancelled or interrupted. Interrupted is a transfer that was running when this server stopped.

storage.description: The storage resource the file came from.

transfer_id.description: The id this server gave the transfer. It is what the stop route and the event stream name it by.

warning.description: What this server could not establish about a transfer that finished, such as a printer that took the file and cannot be asked whether the file is on its storage afterwards. It is a note beside a transfer that succeeded and never a failure, and it is absent for a transfer whose file was confirmed.

reason.description: flag when the server was started with -safe; restart when an administrator asked for a restart in safe mode.

since.description: When this run took safe mode.

path.description: Where the file landed.

sha256.description: The digest the storage took of the bytes it wrote, lowercase hex. Empty for a storage that keeps no digest.

temporary.description: The file is a temporary copy, asked for with temporary=true. Send it to a printer with path as the source. The server deletes it once the file has landed or the transfer was stopped, and one hour after it was written when the send failed, so the same copy can be sent again until then. It is not listed with the storage's files.

transfer.description: The transfer as it ended, including how many bytes this server relayed.

default_id.description: The dashboard the home page draws now, or null.

info.description:
Prusa Connect puts every printer on your network behind one HTTP API. It runs on your own hardware and calls no cloud service.

A printer is never configured here. It dials in over its connector's own wire and this server admits it, so the fleet listing is what has connected rather than what somebody typed into a file. Every printer carries the state it last reported and the verbs this server resolved it accepts. Those verbs are its capability set, narrowed by its model and its firmware, and a command outside the set is refused before the machine is reached.

## The fleet, the stream and one command

`GET /api/v1/devices` answers one page of the devices the caller may see.

`GET /api/v1/events` is the same information as it changes, as a server-sent event stream.

`POST /api/v1/devices/{device_id}/commands` sends one verb from a printer's capability set.

## Credentials and grants

Almost every operation needs a credential this server issued. A browser carries it in the session cookie the login sets, and any other client sends it as a bearer token.

An operation publishing an empty security requirement takes neither. Liveness, readiness, the two login steps and the seven vocabulary operations answer anybody, and nothing else does.

A credential says who the caller is. A grant on one device says what they may do with it, so two callers holding valid credentials see different fleets. `GET /api/v1/grants/device/{object_id}` reads the grants written on one device.

## A refusal carries a code and a trace id

Every failure is an RFC 9457 problem document. Branch on its `code`, which comes from a published set, and never on the wording of `detail`. Quote its `trace_id` to an operator, who can find the same request in the log.

`GET /api/v1/vocabularies/error-codes` lists every code this build can return, with what a caller does about each one.

## The base URL is the origin serving this document

The first server is `/`, which resolves against wherever this document was fetched from. A request sent from this page therefore reaches the deployment being read. A client reading the document outside a browser takes the second server and fills in the host it wants.

post.description:
Answers whether the caller may perform one action on one object, and lists every action they may perform on it. The subject is always the caller: this operation cannot ask about anybody else, and it needs no permission of its own, because a caller may always ask what they themselves may do.

Use it to render an interface: grey a control the caller cannot use, instead of attempting the action to find out. The fleet listing already carries the same set on every printer row, so a client drawing a list of printers does not need this operation at all.

The answer is a hint and never the decision. The server checks the permission again when the action is attempted, and a grant written in between changes what it says. Compare `authorization_epoch` against the value on a cached answer to see whether one has been.

An object this server does not have answers exactly as an object the caller reaches nothing on: `allowed` false and an empty `actions`. That is deliberate, and it is why this operation cannot be used to find out which printers exist.

A body naming a `subject` is refused. Asking what another principal may do is a separate operation with a permission of its own, and this server has none.
post.summary: What the caller may do to one object

The answer sets the session cookie to a page session: an api credential that speaks for the same person with the same scopes, lives at most an hour, and ends when the app's credential is revoked or expires. The cookie is HttpOnly, so no script on the page reads it, and SameSite=Strict. The body carries the same cookie, so an app can put it into its web view itself. The page never holds the credential. Only the header is read: a request that carries the credential in a cookie is refused, so another site cannot open a page session. delete.description:
Marks the device id as no longer naming a machine, for an operator who has taken the printer away. It leaves the fleet listing, because that listing is what is here now, and it is read back with `?retired=include` or `?retired=only`.

Nothing is deleted. The record, the prints, the command log and every grant written on the id stay exactly where they are, so last month's prints are still readable under the id they were filed on, and `GET /api/v1/devices/{device_id}` still answers. That is the whole difference between retiring and deleting. The cameras that watch the printer are the exception: the first retirement removes them, so none keeps running with no printer page to be seen on.

The printer loses its access. The connector takes back the token and the approved fingerprint it issued the printer, so the printer is refused with 401 when it dials again. To come back it has to be added again: Add Printer to Connect on the printer, and an approval where a person approves new printers. A connector that admits every printer checks no credential, so there the printer joins again by itself.

The session is closed where one is open, and the identity this server bound to the machine is released, so a printer admitted again is given a new device id rather than reviving this record. Nothing restores a retired record, and adding the printer again never gives back the old credential. A retirement carries a reason, and this one is `removed_by_operator`; `ownership_changed` is the other, written when a machine that changed hands is registered again.

Retiring twice is the same answer as retiring once, and the second call takes the credential back again in case the first one failed partway. It takes administer on the device, which the manager role confers.

A printer that runs this server has `resident: true` on its record, and its retirement is refused with DEVICE_RESIDENT. Its driver would connect again at once, and the machine would come back under a new id.

Writes the whole tag list, so a tag absent from the body is taken off. A tag is a plain word or short phrase a person puts on a printer, such as `workshop`, `PETG only` or `night shift`. It has no key and no value.

Each tag is trimmed, and a run of spaces inside it becomes one space. The case is kept as sent. A new tag is at most 64 characters, and a device carries at most 32 tags. A comma, a control character and a character that shows nothing are refused, and a tag has at least one visible character. post.description:
Stages a release, reads its manifest, holds the version to the range that was asked for, checks this core is one the module runs on, verifies the digests and writes the declaration into the machine-owned overlay. It is the `module add` command over HTTP, through the same functions and with the same refusals, so a page can install without shell access.

Nothing is written until every check has passed, so a refusal leaves the deployment exactly as it was. Without `approve` the module is installed and switched off, and the answer lists the permissions and the events the manifest asks for: read them, then install again with `approve` or switch the instance on with put-resource. A module the operator declared in their own configuration file is refused, because this server never writes that file.

The install takes effect at once. This server reads the declaration it has just written and converges on it: a module that was switched on starts here, its routes and its bundle are served, and list-resources carries the new instance with its `ui` object, so a page that reads the listing again draws the module's sidebar entry without anybody restarting anything. The answer waits a few seconds for the module to start. `state` says what it reached: `ready` when it is serving, `failed` with the cause in `reason` when it did not start, and `starting` when the start was still going when the wait ended. A module whose settings are missing or refused is `failed`, and the install itself still succeeded: write the settings with put-resource, which starts the module again. `running` is true only when the module is serving, and `restart` is true only when this server still has to be restarted to pick the declaration up.

With no `from`, the release is the one the configured marketplace offers for `module` at exactly `version`, and its digest is the marketplace's. Every fetched release is hashed while it is written and refused with MODULE_DIGEST_MISMATCH when it differs from the stated digest, before anything is unpacked. A `from` URL takes `sha256`. A download is https, and so is every redirect it follows. It never connects to this machine or the local network, except to the port of a marketplace configured on loopback for local development. A download that fails answers MODULE_DOWNLOAD_FAILED, with the same detail whatever the address answered.

With `approve`, the manifest is held to what the operator was shown: what the marketplace lists for the release, and `expect` when the request carries it. A manifest asking for anything beyond either is refused with MODULE_REQUESTS_CHANGED. A release whose name another module already holds is refused with MODULE_NAME_TAKEN.

While the operator's core.modules_enabled is false, every install and every update is refused with MODULES_DISABLED, and in safe mode SAFE_MODE, before anything is read or downloaded.

With `approve`, the install writes the module's grants into the authorization graph, the same grants `module add -approve` writes. A module that asks for observe gets the viewer role on the organization, so it reads every printer. The grants are written as the caller, so the caller needs the admin role on the organization, and an install the graph would refuse writes nothing. The same role is needed whenever `approve` records what the module may do as itself, even a permission no grant answers, `check_absent_people` and `list_people`. `approved` lists what was written and `withheld` what was not.

A reinstall takes back each grant the old declaration justified and the new manifest no longer asks for, and it is refused before anything is written when the caller could not take one back. The graph does not record who wrote a grant, so a grant an administrator wrote by hand that is the same as one of those is taken back too. Installs and removals of modules run one at a time.

Installing over an installed module is the update: the running process is stopped before its files are replaced. With `approve`, an update keeps what the operator decided: a permission or an event they took away stays away, a records room they set is kept unless `records_mib` names another, and `added` lists what the release asks for that the one before did not.

An update is kept only when the new release starts. The release it replaces is kept aside until then, and the answer waits up to a minute, because a module may migrate a database of its own before it reports ready. A new release that fails to start, such as one whose migration failed or one older than its database allows, is taken back: the old files, declaration and grants return, the old release runs again, and the answer is MODULE_UPDATE_ROLLED_BACK with the cause in reason. A migration that fails is undone whole, so the database is as it was. `schema_version` and `migrations` say what a start that succeeded did to the module's own database.

It takes configure_resource on the resource kind the manifest declares, which is the permission to administer that part of this server's configuration.

When `requests_known` is true, `permissions`, `events`, `check_absent_people`, `list_people` and `records_mib` are every request of the release, and a page sends them back as `expect`; when it is false, a page installs without `approve` first and reads the answer's `requests`.

The rows come from the index file in the modules directory and then from the marketplace core.marketplace.url names, for this build's version and platform. The marketplace is read in the background of a request and kept for a few minutes, so a page that opens this list does not wait on it each time; a marketplace that does not answer leaves its last copy, or no rows, and the local rows are still served. `marketplace` says which. A deployment pointing at neither answers an empty list, which is the honest answer for a server with nothing to offer rather than an error a page has to handle. It takes configure_resource on a resource kind, because reading what can be installed is part of administering what is installed. While the operator's core.modules_enabled is false it answers MODULES_DISABLED and reads nothing. In safe mode it answers SAFE_MODE.

delete.description:
Stops the process this core is running for the module, deletes the files that were installed for it, and then takes its declaration out of the machine-owned overlay. The files go before the declaration. A delete that fails then leaves the module installed and the same request finishes the job, instead of a deployment with no declaration and files nobody will collect.

A delete can fail for a moment after the process stops, because the system has not let go of the module's own executable yet. The server waits for that and retries; what outlasts the wait is answered as a conflict naming the directory that is still there, with the module still installed.

A module the operator declared in their own configuration file is refused: remove the block there instead. A namespace nothing declares is a 404. It takes configure_resource on the resource kind the module is declared under.

What stays: the records the module kept in the record store, under its namespace, and its data directory, module-data/<name> beside the modules directory, both of which the same module reads again when it is installed again; a database of the module's own, which list-module-databases lists until purge-module-database deletes it; and every file in a storage, which belongs to the storage and not to the module. What goes: the module's files under the modules directory, its declaration with its settings, and the grants its install wrote.

The module's grants are taken back as the principal the server's configuration names, core.principal, and not as the caller, because taking a grant away gives nobody anything. An install writes them as the caller.

The removal takes effect at once. The instance leaves list-resources and the readiness report in this same request, so a page that reads either again no longer draws the module.

A module another installed module requires is refused with MODULE_REQUIRED_BY, whose requires names each such module and its range. Remove those modules first. With `with_unused`, the modules an install added for this one that nothing else requires any more are removed in the same request; get-module-removal lists them first.
